json.title: The Secret of the Founder's Map
json.logline: Two students with clashing personalities must learn to work together using an ancient map to uncover their town's forgotten history.

characters.name: Angel
characters.description: A meticulous and book-smart 6th grader who loves history and believes every problem can be solved with research and a good plan.

characters.name: Jayson
characters.description: An energetic and creative 5th grader who prefers to act on instinct and is skilled at solving hands-on puzzles.

json.setting: The story is set in the small, historic town of Oakhaven, a place where cobblestone streets meet modern storefronts. The atmosphere is cozy and sleepy, but beneath the surface lie old secrets, particularly within the dusty, forgotten 'Founder's Wing' of the Oakhaven Middle School library, a place filled with the scent of old paper and leather-bound books.

plot_points.title: Opening
plot_points.description: Paired for a history project, studious Angel and impulsive Jayson bicker in the school library, unable to agree on a topic.

plot_points.title: Inciting Incident
plot_points.description: Jayson accidentally knocks a loose book, revealing a hidden compartment containing a cryptic, hand-drawn map signed by the town's founders.

plot_points.title: Rising Action
plot_points.description: They follow the map's trail through Oakhaven, with Angel deciphering historical riddles and Jayson solving physical puzzles, slowly and grudgingly realizing they need each other's different skills to progress.

plot_points.title: Climax
plot_points.description: At the final location, the old clock tower, they face a complex puzzle that requires Angel's code-breaking and Jayson's mechanical tinkering to be performed at the same time, forcing them to finally trust each other completely to succeed.

plot_points.title: Resolution
plot_points.description: They unearth the time capsule, which contains not treasure, but a message about community and collaboration. They present their amazing discovery for their project, earning an A+ and forging a new friendship built on mutual respect for their unique talents.

json.moral_lesson_summary: The successful discovery of the time capsule, achievable only through their combined efforts, teaches Angel and Jayson that true success comes from collaborating and valuing the different skills each person brings to a team.

json.output:
The scent of balsa wood and model glue filled the garage, a smell Angel equated with pure happiness. He hunched over their workbench, a single beam of light from his desk lamp illuminating the delicate skeleton of a glider wing. With the focus of a surgeon, he applied a tiny bead of glue along a join, holding his breath until it set.

“Are you done with that one piece yet?” Jayson’s voice was laced with impatience. He was slumped on a stool across the bench, listlessly spinning a screwdriver on the cement floor. “We’ve been at this for three hours. My eyeballs are starting to dry out.”

“It has to be perfect, Jay,” Angel said without looking up. At twelve, he was a year older than Jayson, and a hundred years more patient. “Look at the blueprint. The curvature of the airfoil has to be exact, or we’ll get turbulence instead of lift.” He ran a gentle finger along the wood. “It’s like an art.”

“It’s like watching paint dry,” Jayson grumbled, kicking at a pile of wood shavings. “The school’s annual Aviation Challenge is in two weeks. At this rate, we’ll have one wing and a note that says, ‘The other one is coming soon.’” He threw his hands up. “There has to be a faster way.”

Angel finally looked at his brother, his brow furrowed. “The whole point is to build it ourselves. That’s the challenge. It’s supposed to take time.”

Jayson sighed, pushing himself off the stool. “I’m gonna go… research fuselage construction techniques.” He headed for the door leading into the house, but Angel knew his brother’s version of research usually involved watching stunt videos online.

Up in his room, Jayson did exactly that for ten minutes before his boredom returned. He begrudgingly typed “model glider kits” into the search bar. He clicked through a few hobby sites, and then he saw it. A banner ad flashed at the top of the screen: “Aero-Glide 5000: Laser-Cut for Perfect Flight. Win Every Time!”

He clicked. The webpage was slick, filled with photos of a stunning, professionally finished glider. The parts were laser-etched balsa wood, promising “unmatched precision” and “flawless aerodynamics.” A complete kit, delivered in two days. It was a shortcut. It was cheating. But the image of that perfect glider soaring through the air, a blue ribbon pinned to its wing, was powerful. He glanced at his piggy bank on the shelf, full of his allowance money. Downstairs, he could hear the soft, rhythmic sound of Angel sanding another piece of wood. So slow. So tedious. With a knot of guilt and excitement tightening in his stomach, Jayson clicked “Add to Cart.”

The package arrived two days later in a plain brown box. Jayson managed to intercept the delivery driver before his mom saw it, smuggling the box up to his room like a secret agent. He waited until Saturday, when Angel was at a friend’s house for the afternoon. With the coast clear, he sprinted to the garage.

He carefully swept their hand-cut, slightly uneven pieces into a shoebox and shoved it under the workbench. Then, he opened the new box. The parts inside were breathtaking. They were smooth, perfect, and smelled faintly of burnt wood from the laser. The pieces fit together with a satisfying click, no sanding required. In less than an hour, the entire glider—fuselage, wings, and tail assembly—was complete. It looked exactly like the one on the website. Professional. Unbeatable.

When Angel got home, he walked into the garage and stopped dead. “Whoa! Jay! You did all this?” He circled the completed glider, his eyes wide with amazement. “How did you get the cuts so clean? And everything lines up perfectly! You must have had a major burst of energy.”

“Yeah, something like that,” Jayson mumbled, avoiding his brother’s eyes. “Just got in the zone, I guess.”

“In the zone? You’re a master builder!” Angel beamed, running a hand reverently over the smooth wing. “We are definitely going to win with this.”

Jayson felt a sharp pang of guilt. Angel’s praise felt like a stone in his gut. This wasn’t their work. It was his lie.

The day of the Aviation Challenge, the school gymnasium buzzed with the chaotic energy of two dozen teams. The air was a cacophony of excited chatter and the faint squeak of sneakers on polished wood. Models of all shapes and sizes sat on display tables—some were clumsy and coated in too much glue, others were sleek and painted with bold racing stripes.

Angel proudly set their glider on their assigned table, polishing an imaginary speck of dust off its nose. He explained the finer points of their "design" to anyone who would listen. Jayson just stood beside him, hands jammed in his pockets, his stomach churning. He couldn't shake the feeling that everyone knew. That their glider was a fraud.

Mr. Harrison, the retired aerospace engineer who judged the competition every year, made his way down their row. He stopped at their table, his kind, crinkly eyes studying their entry. He picked it up, testing its weight and balance.

“Well, now,” he said, his voice a low rumble of approval. “This is a fine piece of work, boys. Just look at that impeccable craftsmanship. Truly professional.”

Angel swelled with pride. “Thanks, Mr. Harrison. We worked really hard on it.”

Jayson just nodded, feeling his face flush with heat. The judge’s compliment felt like an accusation.

Finally, it was their turn to fly. Angel carried the glider to the launch line like it was a sacred relic. “You ready for this?” he whispered to Jayson, his eyes sparkling. Jayson gave a weak thumbs-up.

Angel launched the glider with a smooth, practiced motion. It caught the air instantly, soaring in a long, graceful arc across the gymnasium. It flew further than any other plane, landing with a soft whisper near the far wall. The gym erupted in applause.

“And the winner of this year’s Aviation Challenge,” Mr. Harrison announced into a microphone a few minutes later, “is the team of Angel and Jayson Reyes!”

Angel let out a whoop of joy, grabbing Jayson in a hug. Jayson felt numb as they walked up to the stage to receive the large, golden trophy. As Mr. Harrison handed it to them, he leaned in. “I have to ask,” he said with a smile, “what kind of tool did you use for that laser-cut precision on the wing struts? It’s flawless.”

The words hit Jayson like a physical blow. Angel’s smile faltered. He looked from Mr. Harrison to the glider, then to his brother.

“Laser-cut?” Angel said, his voice small and confused. “We… we used a craft knife and sandpaper.” He stared at Jayson, a dawning horror in his eyes. The pieces clicked together in his head, just like the pieces of the kit. The sudden progress. The perfect cuts. Jayson’s strange, quiet mood. “Jay?”

The whole gym was quiet, watching them. Jayson couldn't look at his brother. He couldn't look at anyone. The lie was too heavy to hold anymore. “I bought it,” he whispered, the words tasting like ash. “It was a kit. I’m sorry.”

The silence that followed was worse than any shouting. Angel’s face crumpled, not with anger, but with a deep, bottomless hurt. He put his half of the trophy down on the stage and walked away without a word.

Back in the garage, the gleaming trophy sat on the workbench between them, an unwelcome intruder. The air was thick with unspoken words. Angel finally broke the silence, his voice quiet.

“I don’t care about the stupid trophy, Jay,” he said, tracing a pattern in the sawdust on the bench. “I cared about building it. With you. That was the fun part.”

Tears welled in Jayson’s eyes. His brother was right. The best moments hadn’t been the idea of winning, but the hours they’d spent together in the garage, laughing over a crooked cut or figuring out a tricky part of the blueprint. The journey, not the destination.

“I know,” Jayson said, his voice choked. “I’m so sorry, Angel. I just wanted to win so badly, I forgot what we were really doing.” He looked at his brother, his apology genuine and raw. “It was dumb. I messed up.”

A long moment passed. Then, Angel nodded slowly. “Yeah. You did.” He looked at the trophy, then back at Jayson. “So, what are we going to do about it?”

Jayson knew what they had to do. The next morning, they returned the trophy to Mr. Harrison with a quiet explanation. Back in the garage, the space felt lighter, cleaner. Jayson reached under the workbench and pulled out the dusty shoebox containing their original, half-finished glider. He placed the imperfect, hand-cut fuselage on the table.

He picked up a piece of sandpaper and looked at his brother.

A small smile touched Angel’s lips. He reached for the bottle of wood glue. “The curvature of the airfoil has to be exact,” he said, his voice filled with its old, patient warmth. And together, they got back to work.
